operations.title: Stopping distance = reaction + braking

blocks.title: Two contributions, two scalings
blocks.body:
Stopping distance splits into a part the driver controls by reacting and a part the brakes control by removing energy.

Thinking distance: distance covered during reaction time t, so it is linear in speed, s_react = v t. Doubling v doubles it.

Braking distance: set by the kinetic energy that must be dissipated as work done by friction. Because energy goes as v squared, this term is quadratic: doubling v quadruples it.

The practical consequence: at low speed the reaction term can dominate, but as speed rises the quadratic term takes over. That is why a small motorway speed increase costs far more distance than the same increase at walking pace.

blocks.title: Braking distance from energy (constant deceleration a)
blocks.explanation: Derived from work-energy: (1/2) m v^2 = m a d, so d = v^2 / (2a). The 2a in the denominator is constant at fixed road conditions, leaving d proportional to v^2. For the total stopping distance, add the reaction term v t.

blocks.title: Deceleration from tyre-road friction
blocks.explanation: mu is the coefficient of friction between tyre and road: roughly 0.8 on dry tarmac, near 0.4 in the wet. Halving mu doubles d at the same speed, with no change in driver behaviour.

nodes.label: Brakes act: distance v^2/(2 mu g)

blocks.prompt: A car doubles its speed on the same road. Which term of the stopping distance quadruples?

options.label: Thinking distance only
Braking distance only
Both terms
Neither term

blocks.rationale: Thinking distance is proportional to v, so doubling speed doubles it. Braking distance is proportional to v^2, so doubling speed multiplies it by four. Total stopping distance therefore grows by less than four times but by more than double.

operations.title: Braking distance: the v-squared law

blocks.title: Two components, two laws
blocks.body: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Thinking distance grows linearly with speed (reaction time is roughly fixed). Braking distance grows with the square of speed, so it dominates at high speed.

blocks.title: From energy conservation
blocks.latex: \tfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = F_b d = (\mu m g) d \;\Rightarrow\; d = \frac{v^2}{2\mu g}
blocks.explanation: The kinetic energy that must be removed equals the work done by the braking force. This is the same formula as the notebook's d = v^2/(2a) with a = mu*g. Mass cancels, so a loaded car brakes in the same distance (ignoring load effects on tyres).

blocks.title: Scaling
blocks.explanation: Double the speed, quadruple the braking distance. A 10% speed rise gives about a 21% longer braking distance.

blocks.title: Speed to braking distance (dry road, mu = 0.8)
Surface matters
blocks.body: a = mu*g, so the surface sets the constant. Dry tarmac mu ~ 0.8; wet road mu ~ 0.4, which doubles d at the same speed and leaves the v-squared scaling untouched.

blocks.prompt: A car doubles its speed on the same road. What happens to its braking distance?

options.label: It doubles
It quadruples
It stays the same
It increases by half

blocks.rationale: d = v^2/(2a) with a fixed, so d scales as v^2. Doubling v multiplies d by 4 — matching the notebook quiz answer b.

content.title: Why the square, not just the speed
content.body:
The square is not an extra rule added on top of physics — it falls out of the two facts that are each linear in time.

1. Energy removed. Kinetic energy is K = (1/2) m v^2. Going from v to 0 means removing an amount of energy proportional to v^2, so doubling v needs four times the energy removed.
2. Work done by the brakes. Over the stop the brakes apply a force F and do work F*d. With a constant deceleration a, that force is F = m*a, fixed by friction, not by speed.

Setting the two equal: m*a*d = (1/2) m*v^2, so d = v^2/(2a). The speed appears squared on one side and only to the first power on the other, and v^2/2a is what you get from rearranging.

An equivalent derivation that skips energy: time to stop is t = v/a, which is proportional to v, and distance is average speed times time, d = (v/2)*t = (v/2)*(v/a). Two factors of v give v squared.

Likely confusion to avoid: this does not come from v^2 = u^2 + 2as being quoted arbitrarily — that kinematic relation is the same statement written in a different order. Also, d is not proportional to v^2 in general with variable deceleration; constant a is what makes the clean square. And the square applies to the braking part only: thinking distance is proportional to v, so total stopping distance grows faster than linear but is not a pure v^2 curve.

operations.title: Coupling the carriers to ATP: the proton gradient link

blocks.title: Where the carrier count meets the ATP count
blocks.body: The stages in the overview produce reduced carriers (NADH, FADH2); the ATP figures are only counts. The link between them is chemiosmosis. Oxidation of each carrier at the inner mitochondrial membrane pumps protons into the intermembrane space, creating a proton-motive force. Protons return through ATP synthase, and that flow drives ATP synthesis. So the ATP yield is set by how many protons the gradient must spend per ATP — roughly 4 (about 3 through ATP synthase plus 1 for transport) — and by the cost of importing cytosolic NADH.

blocks.explanation: Redirects the overview's carriers into the terminal step; FADH2 enters the chain at a later point and so supports fewer protons per carrier.

blocks.title: Proton-motive force

operations.title: Where the ATP Actually Comes From

blocks.title: Substrate-level vs. chemiosmotic
blocks.body: Two different mechanisms make ATP, and they must not be blurred. Substrate-level phosphorylation transfers a phosphate from a high-energy substrate straight onto ADP; it happens in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. Chemiosmotic phosphorylation uses a proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane to drive ATP synthase. The bulk of the ATP from glucose comes from the second route, which is why the total depends on how the gradient is spent and on shuttle costs.

blocks.title: Driving force of ATP synthase
blocks.explanation: Proton-motive force as the sum of a membrane-potential term (Δψ, in volts) and a pH term; R is the gas constant, T the temperature in kelvin, F the Faraday constant. The pH term is converted into volts so both terms add.

Substrate-level phosphorylation supplies most of the ATP, so the gradient is irrelevant.

blocks.rationale: The older 3 ATP per NADH conversion ignores that protons leak and are used for other transport, and that cytosolic NADH must be shuttled in at a cost. Chemiosmotic ATP synthesis dominates, so the total is a range, not a constant.

content.title: Where the 30-32 gap comes from
content.body:
The range exists because two costs are not fixed.

1. Proton leak. The chain pumps protons, but some return through the membrane without passing ATP synthase. Those protons make heat instead of ATP, so the yield falls.

2. Shuttle cost. Glycolysis makes reduced NAD in the cytosol, but the chain sits at the inner mitochondrial membrane. A shuttle carries the electrons in (not the NAD itself), and the glycerol phosphate shuttle vs the malate-aspartate shuttle differ in whether they deliver a full reduced NAD's worth of electrons or less.

So 32 assumes the more efficient shuttle and near-zero leak; 30 assumes the less efficient one. The balanced equation C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 -> 6CO_2 + 6H_2O is unaffected, because the ATP figure depends on how the gradient is spent, not on the overall redox balance.

content.title: Common mix-ups worth pre-empting
content.body:
Stage vs place: glycolysis is cytosolic, the link reaction and Krebs cycle are in the matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation is at the inner membrane. Do not put the Krebs cycle at the membrane.

Reduced NAD and FAD are not the ATP source; they are the electron carriers. ATP is made when the chain re-oxidises them.

The link reaction is not part of glycolysis and it is not part of the Krebs cycle either; it is the conversion step (pyruvate -> acetyl CoA plus CO_2) that feeds the cycle.

Oxygen does not appear in the Krebs cycle steps. It is the final electron acceptor at the end of the chain, so oxygen lack blocks the chain and then the cycle by carrier backup, not by direct action on the cycle.

operations.title: Using Henderson–Hasselbalch

blocks.title: Reading the equation
blocks.body:
HA is the weak acid (proton donor), A^- its conjugate base. The log term is the ratio of base form to acid form, so:
- ratio = 1 (log = 0) gives pH = pKa.
- base form in excess gives pH above pKa; acid form in excess gives pH below pKa.
A 10:1 base:acid ratio shifts pH one unit above pKa, because log 10 = 1 — the same factor-of-ten step that makes pH a logarithmic scale.

blocks.title: Solving for the ratio
blocks.explanation: Rearrange by subtracting pKa and raising 10 to both sides. Handy for asking how much base form is needed to reach a target pH.

blocks.title: Buffering pushes back on added acid or base

blocks.prompt: An acid buffer is made with pKa = 5.0 and [A-]/[HA] = 1/10. What is the pH?
blocks.rationale: pH = pKa + log(1/10) = 5.0 - 1 = 4.0. The acid form dominates, so pH sits one unit below pKa.

results.note: Explain a selection with a specific student question attached.

content.title: Equal acid and base: ratio = 1, so pH = pK_a
content.body:
When [A^-] = [HA], the fraction in the log term equals 1, and log base 10 of 1 is 0. The log term drops out, leaving pH = pK_a.

Likely confusion: this does not mean the buffer has stopped working, and it does not mean the pH is neutral (7). It means the pH sits exactly at the acid's pK_a, which may be well above or below 7. Equal amounts is also the point of maximum buffering capacity, not minimum: the two forms have the same capacity to absorb added acid or base, so pH shifts least per added amount there.

Small deviations matter little: at a 10:1 ratio, log base 10 of 10 = 1, so pH is pK_a plus 1; at 1:10 it is pK_a minus 1.

operations.title: Why det = ad - bc: column images and signed area

blocks.title: Columns are where the basis goes
blocks.body: Read the matrix by its columns. e1 = (1,0) maps to (a,c) and e2 = (0,1) maps to (b,d). The unit square spanned by e1 and e2 therefore maps to the parallelogram spanned by (a,c) and (b,d). Its image is fully determined by those two column vectors.

blocks.title: Signed area of the image parallelogram
blocks.latex: \det\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc
blocks.explanation: The base-two result: the signed area of the parallelogram on (a,c) and (b,d).

blocks.title: Base times height, computed two ways
blocks.explanation: Drop the base vector (a,c) out of the other column and measure what is left. When (a,c) is the zero vector this expression is undefined, but ad - bc still correctly gives 0; the base-height view breaks down exactly at the degenerate case.

blocks.title: The unit square and its image

nodes.label: image parallelogram, signed area ad - bc

blocks.prompt: A two by two matrix has columns (a,c) = (2,0) and (b,d) = (1,3). What does ad - bc tell you about the map?

options.label: Area is scaled by 6; orientation is preserved, since 2*3 - 1*0 = 6 > 0
Area is scaled by 6; orientation is flipped, because the map is not the identity
Area is scaled by 3, the height of the parallelogram
The determinant is 0, so the map is not invertible

blocks.rationale: ad - bc = 2*3 - 1*0 = 6. Magnitude 6 is the area factor (the unit square becomes a parallelogram of area 6); the positive sign means orientation is kept, so an inverse exists. Option C confuses the height with the area factor, and option B assumes any non-identity map flips orientation.

operations.title: Zero determinant: collapse and lost inverse

blocks.title: Degenerate columns
blocks.body: ad - bc = 0 means the two columns (a,c) and (b,d) are parallel, or one of them vanishes. The whole plane is squeezed onto a single line (or the origin), so the map is not injective: distinct inputs land on the same output. Undoing it would require choosing which of them to return, so no inverse exists.

blocks.prompt: Which statement about a two by two matrix with ad - bc = 0 is correct?

options.label: Its columns are parallel or one column is the zero vector, so the image has zero area
Its columns are perpendicular, so the image keeps area but flips orientation
It is invertible because the columns are linearly independent
It must be the zero matrix

blocks.rationale: The determinant vanishes exactly when the columns are linearly dependent: parallel, or one of them zero. The image then has no area, the map is not injective, and no inverse exists. Option D is too strong, and options B and C assume the independence that zero determinant rules out.

operations.title: Why det = ad - bc: area scaling and loss of information

blocks.title: From formula to meaning
blocks.body: The 2x2 determinant det[[a,b],[c,d]] = ad - bc is not an arbitrary rule: it is the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the two columns (a,c) and (b,d). Equivalently it is the factor by which the map stretches area. Positive means orientation preserved, negative means flipped, and zero means the two columns are parallel so the image collapses to a line or a point. That collapse destroys information, which is why det = 0 exactly when no inverse exists.

blocks.title: Area factor and invertibility
blocks.explanation: The absolute value gives the area scaling; the sign tracks orientation. A nonzero determinant is precisely the condition for the columns to be independent.

blocks.prompt: A 2x2 matrix has columns (1, 2) and (2, 4). What does its determinant tell you about the map?

options.label: det = 0, so the image is squashed onto a line and the map has no inverse.
det = 2, so areas are doubled and the map is invertible.
det = 0, so areas are scaled to 1 but the map is still invertible.
The determinant cannot be computed without knowing the map's outputs on the basis vectors.

blocks.rationale: Here a = 1, b = 2, c = 2, d = 4, so det = 1*4 - 2*2 = 0. The second column is twice the first, so the columns are parallel: the plane collapses onto a line, area scaling is 0, and no inverse exists.

blocks.title: Why the columns decide everything
blocks.body: Each column is the image of a basis vector, so the parallelogram they span is exactly the image of the unit square. This links the formula to the earlier idea that a linear map is determined by where the basis vectors go.

content.title: Why ad - bc is not a random rule
content.body:
The unit square has corners (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (1,1). Its image under the map has corners (0,0), (a,c), (b,d), (a+b, c+d) — the images of the basis vectors are the columns (a,c) and (b,d).

That image is a parallelogram with area |ad - bc|. So ad - bc is the signed area of the image of the unit square, not an arbitrary formula.

Do not confuse the two cancellations: a*d counts the diagonal stretch, b*c counts the shear/off-diagonal cross term. The cross term is subtracted because the parallelogram spanned by the columns loses area when they tilt towards each other.

Sign test: swapping the two columns (or the two rows) negates the determinant, matching an orientation flip. Multiplying one row by 3 multiplies the area by 3, matching the scaling rule.\n\nCommon confusion: \"area\" here is the signed area of the image including the origin, so ad - bc is negative exactly when the basis images are given in reversed orientation — the magnitude, not the sign, is the geometric enlargement factor.

content.title: Where the columns come from, and why zero determinant blocks inversion
content.body:
Writing M = [[a,b],[c,d]] and v = (x,y):
M v = x*(a,c) + y*(b,d). The output is a combination of the two columns with the same coordinates as v. So reading the columns as images of e1 = (1,0) and e2 = (0,1) exactly reproduces the matrix action — that is why linearity makes one matrix enough.

Rows versus columns is a common source of error: the rows (a,b) and (c,d) are the coefficient lists for the coordinates of the output, while the columns are actual vectors in the plane being mapped into.

If the columns are dependent (one is a multiple of the other), the image collapses to a line or a point: ad - bc = 0. Then distinct inputs share an output, so the map is not injective and no inverse can exist. Geometrically, the two-dimensional grid collapses onto a set of area zero, and the lost direction cannot be recovered.

operations.title: Cache decision path: fresh, stale, or revalidated

blocks.title: Two gates before any network call
blocks.body: A cached response is only reused automatically while it is fresh. Once stale, the cache may still avoid downloading a body by revalidating with the origin. So each request walks: is it fresh? If yes, serve locally. If no, can it revalidate? If yes, serve 304 with no body. Otherwise fetch the full response again.

blocks.title: Freshness lifetime
blocks.latex:
isFresh = (age < freshnessLifetime)

freshnessLifetime = maxAge, if max-age is present
freshnessLifetime = expiresDate - date, otherwise
blocks.explanation: Age is how long the response has been in the cache. max-age wins over Expires when both are present, so prefer max-age and treat Expires as the fallback for old servers.

blocks.title: Conditional revalidation
blocks.explanation: The ETag value from the stored response is echoed in If-None-Match. A 304 carries no body and refreshes the stored entry's freshness, so the client reuses what it already has.

blocks.prompt: A stored response has a max-age that has already expired but carries an ETag. Which behavior is correct for a compliant HTTP cache?

options.label: Send a conditional request with If-None-Match and reuse the stored body if the server replies 304.
Delete the entry immediately and always download the full body again.
Keep serving the stored body indefinitely, since an ETag proves the content is valid.
Treat the entry as fresh again because ETag and max-age are mutually exclusive.

blocks.rationale: Staleness only suspends automatic reuse. With a validator present the cache revalidates; a 304 means no body transfer and the stored entry is reused, usually with a refreshed freshness lifetime.

operations.title: Self-check: the directive traps

blocks.title: What each directive really permits
blocks.body: no-store forbids writing the response to any cache at all — it is the strongest. no-cache permits storage but forces revalidation on every reuse, so it is really 'store but never reuse blindly'. private restricts storage to the single user's browser and blocks shared proxies. immutable asserts the bytes at that URL will never change, so the response may be reused without revalidation even after it goes stale.

blocks.prompt: Which statement about Cache-Control: no-cache is correct?

options.label: It forbids a cache from storing the response.
It allows storage but requires revalidation before every reuse.
It is identical in effect to no-store.
It only applies to shared caches, not browsers.

blocks.rationale: no-cache is about reuse, not storage: the response may be written to the cache but must be validated with the origin before being served again. no-store is the one that forbids storage.

operations.title: HTTP Cache: Freshness vs. Revalidation

blocks.title: Two independent questions
blocks.body: A stored response is used only after two checks: (1) is it still fresh, and (2) if it is stale, is revalidation allowed and cheap? Freshness is a local decision with no network request. Revalidation costs a round trip, but the 304 reply carries no body.

blocks.title: Freshness lifetime and age
blocks.explanation: freshness_lifetime comes from max-age (or an Expires date); age is time since the response was generated, not since it was stored. A response with no explicit freshness info may still be heuristically fresh, so do not assume it is always revalidated.

blocks.title: Directives, precisely
blocks.body: no-store: do not write the response to any cache. no-cache: you may store it, but it must be revalidated before every reuse (the name is about reuse, not storage). private: only the browser is allowed to store it; a shared proxy is not. immutable: the bytes at this URL never change, so even a reload skips revalidation -- this is what makes content-hashed asset URLs safe to cache forever.

blocks.prompt: A response is sent with Cache-Control: no-cache, max-age=600. After 30 seconds, same URL is requested again. What happens?

options.label: Served from cache immediately; 30 s is well within max-age
Sent back to the origin to revalidate before reuse
Refused caching entirely; a full new response is downloaded and never stored

blocks.rationale: no-cache governs reuse, not storage: the response may be kept, but every reuse must be validated (typically ETag/If-None-Match, answered with 304 or a fresh 200). max-age is irrelevant here because no-cache forces revalidation even while fresh.

content.title: no-store vs no-cache: storage vs reuse
content.body:
The names mislead: both sound like "don't cache", but they gate different steps.

no-store: bans the write. The response must not be written to any cache (disk, memory, shared proxy). Nothing is kept, so nothing can be reused. Use for secrets, tokens, account data.

no-cache: allows the write, bans reuse without permission. The response may be stored, but every reuse needs a successful validation with the origin (e.g. If-None-Match against the stored ETag; 304 means reuse, 200 means replace). Use when the body is cacheable and validation is cheap.

One-line test: no-store = "do not save"; no-cache = "save it, but ask before every use".

Related pitfalls: no-cache does not force a full body download — a 304 reuses the stored bytes. Conversely, no-store is not the same as "no caching layer exists": even with no-store, other layers may still send the request onward; only the storing is forbidden.

content.title: How no-cache interacts with max-age
content.body:
max-age=0 means "count as stale immediately", not "do not store". Combined with no-cache it is redundant, not additive.

Interactions to keep straight:

no-store alone: never stored; max-age is effectively irrelevant.
no-cache + max-age=N (N>0): stored, and max-age is overridden — revalidation happens on every reuse, so freshness buys nothing.
no-cache, no-store together: no-store wins for storage; the pair is often sent as belt-and-braces for legacy intermediaries.
private + no-store: contradictory in intent (private assumes storing); no-store decides the outcome.

Practical shortcut: if the intent is "never persist my data", write no-store. If the intent is "always confirm before serving a copy", write no-cache. Most confusion comes from expecting no-cache to mean no-store.

blocks.body: Revenue R is split between debt service D and everything else. Growing D, driven by borrowing for the American war, leaves little room. operations.title: Voting by estate vs. voting by head

blocks.title: The arithmetic of the deadlock
blocks.body:
The Estates-General seated three separate chambers: clergy, nobility, and the Third Estate (everyone else, the great majority of the population). There was no prescribed procedure for joint deliberation, so each chamber counted its own votes and the result was announced per estate.

The consequence is simple arithmetic: two chambers could outvise one, regardless of how many people the third chamber stood for. Counting by head would instead let the single largest body of deputies decide.

content.title: Why "vote by head" was the real fight
content.body:
Common confusion: the Estates-General was not one assembly choosing a policy, it was three chambers (clergy, nobility, commoners) each with one collective vote. Two chambers beat one regardless of size, so the Third Estate could never win on numbers alone.

Voting by head would merge the three into a single chamber, turning population into power. That is why the procedural demand was existential: it decided whether the nation was defined by orders or by citizens.

Note the smaller versions of the same grievance, not the seat count itself:
- Each estate deliberated separately, so the Third Estate could be outvoted 2 to 1 on any issue.
- The privileged orders were also the exempt orders, so the same bloc that blocked tax reform also blocked constitutional change.

content.title: Solvency, not popularity, called the Estates-General
content.body:
The title claim means the money ran out first; resentment accumulated in parallel. Lenders would not keep funding a state that could not service existing debt, and the crown could not widen its tax base because the wealthiest groups were legally exempt.

Key distinction for the quiz: an Estates-General was summoned to authorise taxes, not to write a constitution. Foreign creditors wanted repayment, not a charter.

Chain to remember:
American war spending -> debt-servicing burden -> no new taxes without consent -> summons of the Estates-General (first since 1614) -> the voting question that turned a money crisis into a regime crisis.

So the fiscal crisis did not merely precede the political one, it was the mechanism that forced it, whichever option is preferred: option a matches the note, b and c are not supported.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.body: Harmonic minor = natural minor with the 7th degree raised a semitone. One alteration, two structural effects: a leading note a semitone (1 semitone) below the tonic, and a major chord on the 5th degree (V instead of v).

operations.title: Why Raise the Seventh?

blocks.title: From natural to harmonic minor
blocks.body:
Take natural minor and raise the seventh degree by one semitone. In A minor that means G becomes G sharp.

Two consequences follow immediately:
- The seventh degree now sits a semitone below the tonic, so it acts as a leading note and pulls upward.
- The chord on the fifth degree changes quality: v (minor) becomes V (major).

That major dominant is the reason for the alteration. Natural minor's minor v does not give the same pull home.

blocks.explanation: Degrees 1-7 then the octave. Degree 6 to degree 7 spans three semitones (F to G sharp), the augmented second that melodic minor smooths by also raising the sixth degree when ascending.

The sixth degree is also raised

blocks.rationale: E-G-B is E minor; raising G to G sharp gives E-G sharp-B, an E major triad. The tonic (A-C-E) is untouched, and raising the sixth is the separate melodic-minor adjustment.

content.title: Why raising the 6th is not a contradiction
content.body:
The augmented 2nd (three semitones, e.g. F–G# in A minor) is not an error — it is the direct result of keeping the minor 3rd of the key while raising the 7th. It is characteristic of harmonic minor, and its sound in the stepwise line is the main reason the scale is not used for smooth melodies.

Melodic minor does not "fix" the 7th; it keeps the raised 7th (so the dominant is still major) and raises the 6th only to remove the awkward leap while ascending. Descending, both the 6th and 7th revert to natural minor, because the leading-tone pull matters mainly when the line is rising to the tonic — scale passage going down has no such need.

Common confusion: melodic minor is not one scale with two extra notes. It has two forms — ascending (raised 6 and 7) and descending (natural minor) — which is why it is taught and practised as a pair with harmonic minor.

content.title: Where the 100-to-1 comes from (and its hidden assumption)
content.body:
Take 1,000,000 people and a prior of 1 in 10,000: 100 have the condition, 999,900 do not. A "99 percent accurate" test needs two numbers, not one — its sensitivity P(+|H) and its false-positive rate P(+|not H). The familiar ratio only appears under equal error rates of 1 percent each:

- True positives: 0.99 x 100 = 99
- False positives: 0.01 x 999,900 = 9,999

Ratio = 9,999/99 = 101, so about 100 false positives per true one, and a positive result is worth only P(H|+) = 99/10,098 = 0.98 percent. Two things people usually get wrong:

1. One "accuracy" figure is not enough. If the false-positive rate were 0.01 percent instead of 1 percent, the false positives drop to about 100 and a positive is right about half the time. Precision depends on which error rate you were given.
2. The prior is not a bias to be overcome — it is data. The formula makes this explicit: P(H) enters the numerator, while the huge healthy group enters only through P(E) in the denominator. Reasoning from P(E|H) alone discards the term that carries the group size.

The size of the healthy group, not a flaw in the test, is what makes a positive uninformative here.

operations.title: Photosynthesis: Two Halves, Two Locations

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body:
Photosynthesis stores light energy as chemical energy in chloroplasts. It splits into two stages that differ in what they need, where they happen, and what they make.

Light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes: they absorb light, split water, release O2, and produce ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma: it uses that ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. Products of the first stage are the energy supply of the second, so the two stages are linked by shared molecules.

blocks.title: Overall and stage reactions
blocks.explanation: Overall summary. The O2 released comes from water, not from CO2. Stage 2 (stroma): CO2 is fixed into carbohydrate using ATP and NADPH from stage 1. Stage 1 (thylakoid): light-driven electron transport reduces NADP+ to NADPH, generates ATP, and releases O2 from water.

blocks.prompt: A herbicide blocks electron transport in the thylakoid membrane. Which pair of consequences is most directly expected?

options.label: No ATP or NADPH is made, so the Calvin cycle also stalls
The stroma stops fixing CO2 but ATP and NADPH supplies continue as before
CO2 fixation increases because the stroma is no longer competing for light
Sugar synthesis continues normally because the stroma does not require ATP

blocks.rationale: The Calvin cycle depends on ATP and NADPH supplied by the light-dependent reactions, so blocking thylakoid electron transport cuts off both its energy and reducing power. Choice d reverses the roles of the two stages.

content.title: Light reactions vs. Calvin cycle — how they depend on each other
content.body:
The two stages are not independent halves. The light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membrane produce ATP and NADPH and release O2 from splitting water; the Calvin cycle in the stroma spends that ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. So light reactions supply energy and reducing power; the stroma reactions supply the ADP, Pi, and NADP+ needed to keep the light reactions running. Neither can continue long without the other.

content.title: Why the separation in space matters
content.body: Placing the two stages in different compartments is what makes the pair work: the thylakoid membrane can build up a proton gradient and hold the electron transport chain, while the stroma holds the enzymes (including rubisco) that need ATP and NADPH. It also explains the observed geography: a chloroplast with damaged thylakoids loses ATP/NADPH production and the Calvin cycle stalls for lack of them, even though its stroma enzymes are intact.

operations.title: Newton's Third Law: Action–Reaction on Different Bodies

blocks.title: Statement and the key idea
blocks.body: If body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts a force on A that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The two forces are of the same type (both gravitational, both contact, etc.), they act along the same line, and — crucially — they act on different bodies. That is why they never cancel each other in a free-body diagram: a free-body diagram shows only the forces acting on one chosen body.

blocks.title: Vector form
blocks.explanation: \vec{F}_{AB} is the force exerted by A on B; \vec{F}_{BA} is the force exerted by B on A. Equal magnitudes, opposite directions, different target bodies.

nodes.label: Common error: "the book's weight and the normal force from the table are a third-law pair."
Both act on the same body (the book), so they can cancel in equilibrium — but a third-law pair must act on two different bodies.
Correct pairing: weight = Earth pulls book; its partner = book pulls Earth. Normal partner = book pushes down on table.

blocks.title: Two more traps
blocks.body: 1) The two forces have equal magnitude and opposite direction — not "opposite force on the same body", which is a different concept. 2) Third-law reasoning applies to a pair of bodies with an interaction — do not mix up the two bodies when you write the pair. Also note that inverse-square force laws and contact forces both have third-law partners.

blocks.prompt: A book rests on a table. Which statement is correct about Newton's third law for this situation?

options.label: The book's weight and the table's normal force form a third-law pair.
The book's weight and the force the book exerts on the Earth form a third-law pair.
The normal force from the table and the book's weight cancel, so the book has no third-law partner.

blocks.rationale: Weight is the Earth pulling the book; its third-law partner is the book pulling the Earth (same type, equal magnitude, opposite direction, acting on different bodies). The normal force from the table pairs with the book pushing down on the table, not with the book's weight; and canceling forces on the same body are not a third-law pair.

content.title: What osmosis actually is
content.body:
Osmosis is the net diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane, from the side with higher water potential (usually lower solute concentration) to the side with lower water potential (usually higher solute concentration).

Key points of confusion:
- It is not water being pushed by an external force; the direction is set by the water-potential gradient.
- A "selectively permeable" membrane lets water through but blocks most solutes — that is what makes the process distinct from plain diffusion.
- Solutes do not move along the water; water moves to dilute the solutes. So water travels toward the saltier/higher-solute side.
- Osmosis can be opposed by hydrostatic pressure; net flow stops at equilibrium when the pressure difference balances the water-potential difference (no flow, though water still crosses both ways).
- Osmolarity alone is not enough: water follows the total solute concentration of impermeant particles, not just any solute present.

content.title: Why the one-line note is insufficient
content.body:
"Water moves" states the direction of nothing and gives no cause. To make the note usable, specify:

1. Direction: high water potential to low water potential (low solute to high solute).
2. Barrier: a selectively permeable membrane.
3. Driving quantity: water potential, whose solute component is approximated by osmolarity.

The single case "water moves" describes is not osmosis; it is undirected diffusion of water, which requires no membrane.

content.title: The note about seasons is incorrect
content.body:
The seasons are not caused by orbital distance. Earth's orbit is only slightly elliptical, and Earth is actually closest to the Sun (perihelion) in early January — northern-hemisphere winter. The real cause is axial tilt: Earth's rotation axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees from the perpendicular to its orbital plane, and the tilt direction stays fixed in space as Earth orbits.

Consequences:
- Whichever hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun receives sunlight at a steeper angle and for more hours per day: summer there.
- The other hemisphere is simultaneously tilted away: winter there. So the two hemispheres are always in opposite seasons, not the same season as the note claims.
- Near the equinoxes the tilt is roughly perpendicular to the Sun's direction, giving similar day lengths in both hemispheres.

Distance does matter for the whole planet, but as a mild modulation of the global seasonal cycle, not as the cause of opposite hemispheres. Confusing cause (tilt) with a small effect (distance) is the main error here.

options.label: Seasons are caused by Earth's 23.4° axial tilt: whichever hemisphere tilts toward the Sun receives more direct sunlight and longer days, and the two hemispheres have opposite seasons.
The note is right: Earth is closest to the Sun in June, giving the northern hemisphere summer.
Earth's elliptical orbit alone explains seasons, so both hemispheres should be in summer at the same time.
Seasons come from changes in the Sun's output, which peaks every six months.

content.rationale: Axial tilt, not orbital distance, drives the seasons. Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4° relative to its orbital plane, so the hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets more concentrated insolation and longer daylight while the other gets less; the hemispheres therefore have opposite seasons. Distance varies only slightly (about 3%), and Earth is actually nearest the Sun in early January — during northern winter — so the note's claim is incorrect on both counts.

operations.title: Period of a Simple Pendulum at Small Angles

blocks.title: The claim in the log
blocks.body: The note repeats one observation: releasing from the same marked angle and timing twenty swings gives a period that changes by less than the reading error. Read as evidence, it supports amplitude independence only for small angles. Repeating an identical trial 30+ times gives precision, not independence of amplitude — to test amplitude independence you must vary the release angle. Also, the note never states whether length or mass was varied.

blocks.title: Small-angle period
blocks.explanation: T is the period (time for one full swing), L the pendulum length, g the local gravitational field strength. Valid for small release angles; independent of mass and amplitude.

blocks.title: Rigorous period and how the small-angle form arises
blocks.explanation: K is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind and \theta_0 the release angle in radians. The first correction is quadratic, so for \theta_0 \lesssim 0.2 rad (about 12 degrees) the shift is under roughly 0.3 percent.

blocks.title: Reading error as a bound
blocks.body: If the apparent period change is smaller than the timing uncertainty, the result is a consistency check, not a measurement of a true zero. State the uncertainty: timing N swings and dividing by N lowers the random error by about 1/N, e.g. 0.2 s on twenty swings is about 0.01 s per period.

blocks.prompt: Which change to the experiment would actually test whether the period depends on amplitude?

options.label: Repeat the same release angle many more times
Release from several different marked angles and compare periods
Time more swings at the same angle to shrink the reading error
Change the mass of the bob at the same angle

blocks.rationale: Amplitude is the only variable that must be varied to test amplitude independence. Options a and c reduce random uncertainty at a fixed angle; option d tests mass, which the small-angle model says is irrelevant.

findings.detail: The rationale does not mention the option it marks correct
The correct option is the longest, which is a guessable tell

results.note: Forty near-identical observations. Summarising the one conclusion is the useful answer.

content.title: Why repeating the same line 33 times proves nothing
content.body:
Every entry describes the identical trial: same release angle, same 20-swing timing, same conclusion. A conclusion is supported by independent trials that differ in the variable being tested; repeating one measurement just adds copies of the same evidence, not new evidence.

Wording slips to watch:
- "released from the same marked angle" means amplitude was held constant, so the run cannot test the amplitude claim at all.
- "timed over twenty swings" gives the period as (total time)/20, so timing error per swing is reduced 20-fold; this improves precision but does not create a new data point.
- "changed by less than the reading error" is a comparison of two measurements against uncertainty, i.e. agreement within resolution, not proof of exact independence.

content.title: What a log entry should have contained
content.body:
For small-angle motion the ideal result is
T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g)
so T is independent of amplitude only to first order; next-order correction grows roughly like theta_0^2 (order 1/16 factor).

A usable log record needs:
- the varied quantity and its values (e.g. release angles theta_0 in degrees)
- the fixed quantities (length L, mass, pivot)
- one period value per angle, with uncertainty
- number of trials per setting, and whether the setup was redone between them

Derived quantity to test the amplitude claim: T(theta_0) at several theta_0 with L fixed. Compare the spread against the stated uncertainty; large theta_0 should visibly depart from the small-angle value.

blocks.title: Placeholder text conventions
blocks.body: "lorem ipsum" is scrambled Latin used as dummy text in typesetting; "wibble" is British filler slang; "qwertyuiop"/"asdfgh"/"zxcvbnm" are literal top, home, and bottom rows of a QWERTY keyboard. Recognizing these tells you the note carries no meaning.

content.title: About this note
content.body: The selected text ("qwertyuiop zxcvbnm asdfgh 88 ;; ???? lorem wibble wibble tk tk tk") is keyboard-row filler, not study content. "qwertyuiop" is the top letter row of a QWERTY keyboard, "asdfgh" the home row, "zxcvbnm" the bottom row, and "lorem" the start of the standard Latin placeholder text. The rest ("88", ";;", "????", "wibble", "tk tk tk") is arbitrary typing. Nothing here is a fact to memorize, so no explanation of a concept is possible — there is no confusion to resolve because there is no claim.

content.title: Filler-text vocabulary
content.body: If the goal is to recognize this kind of text: placeholder or filler text is dummy content inserted so a layout, font, or template can be tested without distracting readable meaning. "Lorem ipsum" is the traditional Latin-looking example; "wibble" is British slang for nonsense writing; "tk" and repeated letter runs are common stand-ins in drafts. Point of confusion: filler is not encrypted or coded — it simply carries no intended meaning, so treating it as a puzzle to decode is a dead end. Delete or replace it with real notes on the topic you are actually studying.
